solution:
For raw data, Range \(= x_{\max} - x_{\min}\).

Here the largest observation is \(105\) and the smallest is \(57\).

Range \(= 105 - 57 = 48\)

Range \(= 48\)
_note: The book prints the data list ABOVE the instruction "Find the range for the following data.", so the instruction reads as if it belonged to Q2. Solved as the range question it is.

solution:
This is a discrete frequency distribution, so the range depends only on the VALUES taken, not on their frequencies.

Largest wage \(= 40\), smallest wage \(= 10\) (both in '00 Rs.).

Range \(= 40 - 10 = 30\)

Range \(= 30\) (in '00 Rs.), i.e. Rs. \(3000\)

For a continuous (grouped) distribution,

Range \(=\) upper limit of the highest class \(-\) lower limit of the lowest class.

Highest class is \(165\)-\(175\) and lowest class is \(115\)-\(125\).

Range \(= 175 - 115 = 60\)

Range \(= 60\)

_note: The stem says "100 matches" but the printed frequencies total 90 (5+20+25+15+20+5). Solved from the frequencies actually given, i.e. with N = 90. The book's printed answer 1.35 also uses N = 90 -- it arises from rounding the mean to 2.44 before squaring; carrying the mean unrounded gives 1.34.

solution:
Here \(n = 20\), wrong \(\bar{x} = 20\), wrong \(\sigma = 5\).

Wrong \(\Sigma x = 20 \times 20 = 400\). Replacing the misread \(30\) by the true \(13\):

Correct \(\Sigma x = 400 - 30 + 13 = 383\), so corrected \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{383}{20} = 19.15\)

From \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\Sigma x^2}{n} - (\bar{x})^2\): \(25 = \dfrac{\Sigma x^2}{20} - 400 \Rightarrow \Sigma x^2 = 20(425) = 8500\)

Correct \(\Sigma x^2 = 8500 - 30^2 + 13^2 = 8500 - 900 + 169 = 7769\)

Corrected \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{7769}{20} - (19.15)^2 = 388.45 - 366.7225 = 21.7275\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{21.7275} \approx 4.66\)

Corrected mean \(= 19.15\) cm, corrected S.D. \(\approx 4.66\) cm

For the first \(50\) observations: \(\Sigma x = 50 \times 40 = 2000\)

and from \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\Sigma x^2}{n} - (\bar{x})^2\): \(25 = \dfrac{\Sigma x^2}{50} - 1600 \Rightarrow \Sigma x^2 = 50(1625) = 81250\)

Adding \(60\) and \(72\):

New \(\Sigma x = 2000 + 60 + 72 = 2132\), so new \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{2132}{52} = 41\)

New \(\Sigma x^2 = 81250 + 3600 + 5184 = 90034\)

New \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{90034}{52} - 41^2 = 1731.42 - 1681 = 50.42\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{50.42} \approx 7.1\)

Mean \(= 41\), S.D. \(\approx 7.1\)

Let \(n_1\) be the number of boys and \(n_2\) the number of girls, so \(n_1 + n_2 = 200\).

Here \(\bar{x}_1 = 70\), \(\bar{x}_2 = 62\), \(\bar{x} = 65\), \(\sigma_1 = 8\), \(\sigma_2 = 10\).

From \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{n_1\bar{x}_1 + n_2\bar{x}_2}{n_1+n_2}\):

\(70n_1 + 62(200 - n_1) = 65(200) \Rightarrow 8n_1 = 13000 - 12400 = 600 \Rightarrow n_1 = 75\)

So there are \(75\) boys and \(125\) girls.

Deviations of the group means: \(d_1 = 70 - 65 = 5\), \(d_2 = 62 - 65 = -3\).

\(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{n_1(\sigma_1^2 + d_1^2) + n_2(\sigma_2^2 + d_2^2)}{n_1 + n_2} = \dfrac{75(64+25) + 125(100+9)}{200} = \dfrac{6675 + 13625}{200} = 101.5\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{101.5} \approx 10.07\)

Number of boys \(= 75\), combined S.D. \(\approx 10.07\) inches

For the boys: \(\bar{x}_B = 60\), \(\sigma_B = \sqrt{16} = 4\)

C.V.\(_B = 100 \times \dfrac{4}{60} \approx 6.67\)

For the girls: \(\bar{x}_G = 47\), \(\sigma_G = \sqrt{9} = 3\)

C.V.\(_G = 100 \times \dfrac{3}{47} \approx 6.38\)

The greater C.V. means the greater relative variability.

C.V.\(_B \approx 6.67 >\) C.V.\(_G \approx 6.38\), so the weights of the boys are more variable.

For Brand-I: \(\bar{x}_1 = 36\), \(\sigma_1 = 8\)

C.V.\(_{\text{I}} = 100 \times \dfrac{8}{36} = \dfrac{200}{9} \approx 22.22\)

For Brand-II: \(\bar{x}_2 = 48\), \(\sigma_2 = 10\)

C.V.\(_{\text{II}} = 100 \times \dfrac{10}{48} = \dfrac{125}{6} \approx 20.83\)

Interpretation: Brand-I has the larger C.V., so the life of Brand-I watches varies more; Brand-II is the more consistent brand and also has the higher average life (\(48\) months against \(36\)).

C.V.\(_{\text{I}} \approx 22.22\), C.V.\(_{\text{II}} \approx 20.83\); Brand-I is more variable.

solution:
Area (\(n = 7\)): \(\Sigma x = 973\), so \(\bar{x} = \dfrac{973}{7} = 139\)

Deviations \(x - 139\): \(17, -4, -11, -22, 2, 15, 3\), giving \(\Sigma(x-\bar{x})^2 = 289+16+121+484+4+225+9 = 1148\)

\(\sigma_x^2 = \dfrac{1148}{7} = 164\), so \(\sigma_x = \sqrt{164} \approx 12.81\)

C.V.\(_x = 100 \times \dfrac{12.81}{139} \approx 9.21\)

Yield (\(n = 7\)): \(\Sigma y = 481\) and \(\Sigma y^2 = 33171\), so \(\bar{y} = \dfrac{481}{7} \approx 68.71\)

\(\sigma_y^2 = \dfrac{33171}{7} - \left(\dfrac{481}{7}\right)^2 = \dfrac{836}{49} \approx 17.06\), so \(\sigma_y = \sqrt{17.06} \approx 4.13\)

C.V.\(_y = 100 \times \dfrac{4.13}{68.71} \approx 6.01\)

C.V.\(_x \approx 9.21 >\) C.V.\(_y \approx 6.01\), so the variation is greater in the area of the field.
_note: DISAGREE with the printed key on the yield C.V. The book gives (C.V.)_Y = 5.91; the correct value is 6.01. Check: Sigma y = 481 and Sigma y^2 = 33171 over n = 7, so mean = 481/7 = 68.7143 and variance = (7(33171) - 481^2)/49 = 836/49 = 17.0612, giving sigma = 4.1305 and C.V. = 100(4.1305)/68.7143 = 6.011. The book's area value 9.21 is correct, and the stated conclusion (variation greater in the area) is unchanged either way.
